title: A Red, Red Rose
html:
"A Red, Red Rose" is probably the best-known love song in the English language, and it is barely sixteen lines long. Robert Burns took two old Scottish folk songs, reshaped them, and produced a lyric that says only one thing — I love you and I will not stop — but says it with such music that it has been sung for more than two hundred years. This unit looks at how so plain a statement is made so memorable.

What the exam wants from this poem

Know the two similes of the first stanza, the three impossible conditions of stanzas two and three, and the turn to farewell in stanza four. Be able to name the form (ballad stanza, ABCB) and to explain why exaggeration here sounds sincere rather than silly.

9.1 About the poet

Robert Burns (25 January 1759 – 21 July 1796) is the national poet of Scotland. He was born at Alloway in Ayrshire, the eldest son of a poor tenant farmer, and he spent his short life close to the hard farm work that ruined his health. He died at Dumfries at the age of thirty-seven.

Burns published his first collection, Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect (known as the Kilmarnock edition), in 1786. Its success made him famous overnight in Edinburgh, where he was admired — and patronised — as the "heaven-taught ploughman". His major poems include "Tam o' Shanter", "To a Mouse", "To a Louse", "Ae Fond Kiss", "Scots Wha Hae" and "Auld Lang Syne", which is still sung across the world at the turn of the year. In his last years he worked without payment on two great song collections, James Johnson's The Scots Musical Museum and George Thomson's Select Collection, hunting down old Scottish airs and writing new words for them. "A Red, Red Rose" (1794) came out of exactly that work: Burns himself described it as a simple old song which he had taken down and set to music.

Burns wrote in Scots, the language of ordinary Ayrshire speech, at a time when polished English was expected of poets. That choice, together with his interest in strong personal feeling, folk song and the lives of the poor, makes him a forerunner of the Romantic movement; Wordsworth and Coleridge, whose Lyrical Ballads appeared two years after Burns's death, admired him greatly. Scotland still keeps his birthday as Burns Night.

9.2 Summary

Stanza 1 — Two similes

O my Luve's like a red, red rose, That's newly sprung in June; O my Luve's like the melodie That's sweetly play'd in tune.

The speaker compares his beloved to two things. First to a rose — not any rose, but a red one that has just opened in June, so the comparison carries colour, freshness, perfection and the height of summer. Then to a melody sweetly played in tune. The first comparison appeals to the eye, the second to the ear; the first is a thing of nature, the second a thing of art. Together they say that the beloved is both beautiful to look at and harmonious to live with.

Stanza 2 — The first vow

As fair art thou, my bonnie lass, So deep in luve am I; And I will luve thee still, my dear, Till a' the seas gang dry.

Now the speaker moves from description to promise. The construction is careful: as beautiful as you are, so deeply am I in love — his love is measured by her beauty. He then swears to go on loving her until all the seas dry up, which is to say for ever, since the seas will not dry up.

Stanza 3 — The vow made larger

Till a' the seas gang dry, my dear, And the rocks melt wi' the sun; And I will luve thee still, my dear, While the sands o' life shall run.

The stanza opens by repeating the last line of stanza two, so the two stanzas lock together like links in a chain — a device taken straight from folk song. The impossible condition is then raised higher: not only until the seas dry, but until the very rocks melt in the heat of the sun. The last line quietly changes the measure from the life of the earth to the life of a man: he will love her while "the sands o' life shall run", that is, as long as the sand keeps falling through the hourglass of his own life.

Stanza 4 — The farewell

And fare-thee-weel, my only Luve! And fare-thee-weel, a while! And I will come again, my Luve, Tho' 'twere ten thousand mile!

Only in the final stanza do we learn that the lovers are about to be separated. The whole poem has in fact been a parting speech. The speaker says goodbye twice, then softens it at once with "a while" — this is not an ending but an interval — and promises to return even if ten thousand miles lie between them. The poem closes on movement towards the beloved rather than away from her, which is why it feels joyful and not sad.

9.3 Themes

The intensity of young love. The poem does not analyse love or doubt it. It simply declares it at full volume, with the confidence of a folk singer rather than the caution of a philosopher.

Love against time. Every vow in the poem is a vow about duration. Seas, rocks and sand are all images of time — geological time in the first two, a human lifetime in the third. Love is set against the largest clocks the speaker can imagine, and claims to outlast them.

Beauty and nature. The beloved is praised only through natural and musical images: a June rose, a tune. Burns finds the language of love in the countryside he worked in, not in classical mythology.

Separation and constancy. The parting of the last stanza gives the poem its occasion. Distance is admitted — ten thousand miles of it — and then dismissed. Constancy is the proof of love, and absence is the test it must pass.

The folk tradition. Repetition, simple diction, the linking of stanzas and the singable rhythm all come from oral song. The poem belongs to ordinary people, and that is part of what it is saying about love.

9.4 Form, structure and rhyme

Stanza form. Four quatrains (four-line stanzas) in the ballad stanza, also called common metre — the oldest and most singable stanza in English and Scots verse.

Metre. The long lines are in iambic tetrameter (four iambs) and the short lines in iambic trimeter (three iambs). An iamb is a foot of two syllables, an unstressed one followed by a stressed one — the sound da-DUM. Scanning line 1:

O my | Luve's like | a red, | red rose

Four feet, eight syllables. Line 2 has three:

That's new- | ly sprung | in June

Two small irregularities are worth noticing, because examiners like them. In line 1 "red, red rose" wants a stress on both reds, so the third foot pushes against the iambic beat and the repetition is pressed on our attention. And in stanza 3 the short lines carry an extra light syllable ("And the rocks melt wi' the sun"), which keeps the singing rhythm from becoming mechanical.

Rhyme scheme. ABCB in every stanza — only the second and fourth lines rhyme:

  • Stanza 1: rose (A), June (B), melodie (C), tune (B)
  • Stanza 2: lass (A), I (B), dear (C), dry (B)
  • Stanza 3: dear (A), sun (B), dear (C), run (B)
  • Stanza 4: Luve (A), while (B), Luve (C), mile (B)

What the form does for the meaning. The half-rhymed ABCB pattern leaves the long lines free and un-tied, so the poem moves forward easily, the way speech and song do, while the returning B rhyme gives just enough closure to each stanza. The alternation of four beats and three leaves a silent beat at the end of every short line — exactly the gap a singer fills with the tune. And the chain link between stanzas 2 and 3, where the last line of one becomes the first line of the next, is a technique of oral ballad: it makes the vow sound repeated, sworn twice, the way real promises are.

Answering a "form" question

Never answer only "it is a four-stanza poem". Name the ballad stanza, name iambic tetrameter and trimeter, write out ABCB, quote one line to show the da-DUM beat, and finish with one sentence on what the form achieves. Those five moves are the five marks.

9.5 Poetic devices

Device Example Effect
Simile "my Luve's like a red, red rose" Gives the beloved the colour, freshness and perfection of a flower at its peak
Simile "like the melodie / That's sweetly play'd in tune" Adds sound to sight: she is harmony as well as beauty
Metaphor "the sands o' life" Life becomes an hourglass, so the vow is measured against the speaker's own death
Personification "the rocks melt wi' the sun" The stubborn earth is made to give way, as if nature itself could be overcome by time
Hyperbole "Till a' the seas gang dry"; "ten thousand mile" Deliberate exaggeration that measures love against impossibility
Alliteration "red, red rose"; "sweetly ... sprung" The repeated consonants make the lines sing and slow the reader on the key words
Imagery the June rose, dry seas, melting rocks, running sand Abstract love is made visible in four sharp pictures
Enjambment "O my Luve's like a red, red rose, / That's newly sprung in June" The sense runs over the line-break, so the voice flows instead of stopping
Repetition "red, red"; "fare-thee-weel ... fare-thee-weel"; "my dear" Insistence; the mark of a song rather than a speech
Refrain / chain link "Till a' the seas gang dry" ending stanza 2 and opening stanza 3 Binds the stanzas and makes the promise sound sworn twice
Symbolism the red rose Beauty, passion and love — but also, since roses fade, the pressure of time behind the poem
Dialect (Scots) "Luve", "bonnie lass", "gang", "wi'", "a'" Roots a universal feeling in a real place and a real speaking voice
Apostrophe "O my Luve"; "fare-thee-weel, my only Luve!" The beloved is addressed directly, so we overhear a conversation, not a description

9.6 Glossary

Word Meaning
Luve love; Burns uses it both for the feeling and for the beloved person
newly sprung just come into flower
melodie melody, tune
play'd played (the apostrophe marks a dropped letter, as in song)
in tune correctly pitched; in harmony
fair beautiful
art thou are you (old second-person singular)
bonnie pretty, fine, healthy-looking (Scots)
lass girl, young woman (Scots)
thee you (object form, old singular)
still always, continually — not "even now"
a' all (Scots)
gang go (Scots); "gang dry" = run dry
wi' with
sands o' life the sand in an hourglass, standing for the time a person has to live
fare-thee-weel farewell, goodbye
a while for a short time only
Tho' 'twere though it were
ballad stanza a four-line stanza rhyming ABCB, with lines of four and three beats
iamb a metrical foot of one unstressed then one stressed syllable (da-DUM)

Chapter summary

  • "A Red, Red Rose" (1794) by Robert Burns is a four-stanza Scots love song built from older folk material.
  • Stanza 1 praises the beloved with two similes (a newly opened red rose; a sweetly played melody); stanzas 2 and 3 swear love until the seas dry, the rocks melt, and the speaker's own life runs out; stanza 4 turns out to be a farewell with a promise to return across ten thousand miles.
  • Form: four quatrains in the ballad stanza, alternating iambic tetrameter and iambic trimeter, rhyming ABCB.
  • Central devices: simile, hyperbole, symbolism of the rose, repetition and the chain link between stanzas 2 and 3.
  • Themes: the intensity of love, love against time, beauty drawn from nature, constancy in separation, and the folk-song tradition.
  • The Scots dialect and the singable rhythm are not decoration; they are why a very simple statement has lasted more than two centuries.

Practice questions

Short answer questions (2 marks each)

  1. To what two things does the speaker compare his beloved in the first stanza, and why are both needed? [2]
  2. What impossible conditions does the speaker use to describe how long he will love? [2]
  3. What does the phrase "the sands o' life" mean, and what does it add to the poem? [2]
  4. Why does the poem end with a farewell? [2]
  5. Write the rhyme scheme of the poem and name its stanza form. [2]
  6. Identify the metre of the poem and scan the line "O my Luve's like a red, red rose". [2]
  7. Why does Burns write in the Scots dialect? [2]
Model answers — short questions

1. He compares her to a red rose that has just opened in June, and to a melody sweetly played in tune. The first is an image for the eye and suggests colour, freshness and perfection; the second is an image for the ear and suggests harmony and sweetness. Together they praise both how she looks and how she makes him feel.

2. He says he will love her till all the seas run dry, till the rocks melt in the sun, and for as long as the sands of his own life keep running. Since none of the first two can happen, the vow means "for ever", measured against the age of the earth and then against his own lifetime.

3. It refers to the sand falling through an hourglass, and so means the time a person has left to live. It brings the huge, geological exaggerations of the earlier lines back to a human scale, and quietly admits that the speaker himself is mortal even while his love claims to be endless.

4. The whole poem turns out to be a parting speech: the lovers are about to be separated. The farewell explains why the speaker has been swearing constancy, and because he says goodbye only "a while" and promises to return "tho' 'twere ten thousand mile", the poem ends looking forward to reunion rather than to loss.

5. The rhyme scheme is ABCB in each of the four stanzas — only the second and fourth lines rhyme (June/tune, I/dry, sun/run, while/mile). The stanza form is the ballad stanza, or common metre: a quatrain of alternating four-beat and three-beat lines.

6. The metre alternates iambic tetrameter and iambic trimeter. The line scans as four iambs: "O my | Luve's like | a red, | red rose" — da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM. The repeated "red" pulls an extra stress into the third foot, which is a deliberate variation.

7. Scots was the everyday speech of the Ayrshire country people Burns lived and worked among. Using it keeps the poem close to real speech and to oral folk song, gives it a distinct music ("gang", "bonnie", "a'"), and asserts the dignity of ordinary Scottish life at a time when poets were expected to write polished English.

Long answer questions (5 marks each)

  1. Discuss how Burns uses hyperbole in "A Red, Red Rose". Does the exaggeration weaken the poem or strengthen it? [5]
  2. Show how the form of "A Red, Red Rose" — its stanza, metre, rhyme and repetitions — supports what the poem says. [5]
  3. "A Red, Red Rose is a poem about time as much as about love." Discuss. [5]
Model answers — long questions

1. Hyperbole — deliberate exaggeration — is the engine of the poem's second half. The speaker promises to love "till a' the seas gang dry", until "the rocks melt wi' the sun", and to return even if "ten thousand mile" separate them. Taken literally these are absurd; nobody expects oceans to evaporate. But the poem is a song, not a contract, and the exaggeration is doing emotional work rather than factual work. Each image is drawn from the most permanent things the speaker can think of — the sea, the rock, the sun — so that love is measured against the largest and most unchanging objects in the world, and still claims to outlast them. The exaggerations also escalate: the seas drying is followed by something even less likely, rocks melting, and the chain link between the stanzas makes the vow sound sworn twice. What saves the poem from sounding foolish is the plainness of everything around the hyperbole: simple Scots words, a folk-song rhythm, and the very human admission of "the sands o' life", which reminds us that the speaker will die. The exaggeration therefore strengthens the poem. It does not ask us to believe the seas will dry; it asks us to feel how much a young man in love needs to say that they might.

2. Burns chooses the ballad stanza — four quatrains of alternating iambic tetrameter and trimeter, rhyming ABCB — and every feature of it serves the meaning. The metre is the da-DUM of ordinary English and Scots speech, so the declaration sounds spoken rather than composed. The short three-beat lines leave a silent fourth beat at the end of each, the natural gap for a singer's tune, which is why the poem has been sung for two centuries. Rhyming only the second and fourth lines leaves the long lines free to run on, giving the movement of easy speech while the returning rhyme still rounds each stanza off. Repetition works at three levels: inside the line ("red, red"), inside the stanza ("fare-thee-weel … fare-thee-weel"), and between stanzas, where the last line of stanza 2 becomes the first line of stanza 3 — the chain link of oral ballad, which makes the promise sound repeated and therefore binding. Small departures from the metre carry meaning too: the double stress on "red, red rose" presses the colour on us, and the extra light syllable in stanza 3's short lines keeps the song from becoming mechanical. The structure moves from description (stanza 1) to vow (stanzas 2–3) to farewell (stanza 4), so the form delivers the surprise of the ending. Simple feeling is given a simple, perfect shape.

3. The subject of the poem looks like love, but almost every line is really about duration. Stanza 1 already contains time: the rose is "newly sprung in June", caught at the exact moment of perfection — and any reader knows that a June rose has a fortnight to live. The praise therefore carries its own shadow. The middle stanzas answer that shadow by measuring love against the biggest clocks the speaker knows: the seas will have to dry and the rocks melt before his love changes. These are geological spans, far beyond a human life, and they are invoked precisely because they are beyond it. Then stanza 3 turns the measure inward — he will love "while the sands o' life shall run", an hourglass image that brings us from the age of the earth back to one man's mortality, honestly admitted. The last stanza changes the unit again, from time to distance and back: the parting is only "a while", and the ten thousand miles will be crossed. The poem's real argument, then, is that love is the one human thing willing to stand up against time, even though the lover knows perfectly well that the rose fades and the sand runs out. Its confidence is moving because it is not ignorant.

Reference to the context

  1. Read the following stanza and answer the questions.

    O my Luve's like a red, red rose, That's newly sprung in June; O my Luve's like the melodie That's sweetly play'd in tune.

(a) Name the figure of speech used twice here. (b) Why is the rose described as "newly sprung in June"? (c) What does the second comparison add that the first cannot? [5] 2. Read the following stanza and answer the questions.

And fare-thee-weel, my only Luve! And fare-thee-weel, a while! And I will come again, my Luve, Tho' 'twere ten thousand mile!

(a) What situation does this stanza reveal? (b) Identify one example of hyperbole and one of repetition. (c) Why does the poem not end sadly? [5]

Model answers — reference to the context

1. (a) Simile — the comparisons are made openly with the word "like", first to a rose and then to a melody. (b) June is the height of the Scottish summer and "newly sprung" means the flower has only just opened. The beloved is therefore compared not to a rose in general but to a rose at the single moment of its greatest freshness, colour and perfection. The detail also hints, without saying so, at how briefly such perfection lasts — which is why the rest of the poem is so concerned with lastingness. (c) The rose is seen; the melody is heard. The second simile moves the praise from sight to sound, and from nature to art. A tune "sweetly play'd in tune" suggests harmony, order and rightness, so the beloved is not only beautiful to look at but pleasing to be with. Between them the two similes praise her whole effect on the speaker.

2. (a) It reveals, for the first time, that the lovers are about to be separated: the speaker is leaving, and the entire poem has been a parting speech rather than a general praise of love. (b) Hyperbole: "ten thousand mile", a deliberately enormous distance. Repetition: "fare-thee-weel" is repeated in consecutive lines (and "my Luve" twice in the stanza), giving the insistence of a song. (c) Because the farewell is immediately limited and then cancelled. "A while" turns the goodbye into a short interval, and the last two lines promise return in spite of any distance. The stanza therefore ends on the idea of coming back, not of going away, and the final movement of the poem is towards the beloved.
